# ClipStack

> A menu bar clipboard history manager for macOS. Press ⌥⌘V to reopen
> everything you have copied — text, links and images — and paste any of it
> straight back into the app you were working in. One-time purchase of $12
> with a 14-day free trial. Clipboard history is stored locally and never
> leaves the Mac.

## What it is

ClipStack is a native macOS utility written in Swift. It lives in the menu
bar with no Dock icon and no windows. It captures every copy automatically
and keeps a searchable history you reopen with a global shortcut.

## Key facts

- Platform: macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later
- Architecture: universal binary — native on Apple Silicon and Intel
- Price: $12 USD, one-time purchase. Not a subscription.
- Trial: 14 days, full features, no card required
- Refunds: 30-day money-back guarantee
- Download size: 2.1 MB; about 17 MB of memory in use
- Distribution: direct download, signed and notarized by Apple
- Payment: Lemon Squeezy is the merchant of record

## Features

- Automatic capture of text and images; nothing to press first
- Global ⌥⌘V shortcut opens the panel at the pointer
- Pastes back into the app you were using, not merely onto the clipboard
- Pin items so they are never pushed out by newer copies
- Type-to-filter, plus All / Text / Images / Links tabs
- ⌘1 through ⌘9 paste the nth item instantly
- Ignores copies that password managers mark as confidential
- Optional start at login

## Privacy

Clipboard history is a local JSON file in the user's Library folder. There
is no account, no sync, no analytics and no telemetry, and nothing that is
copied is ever transmitted. The app makes two kinds of network request: a
once-daily check for a new version, and a licence verification on activation
and roughly once a month thereafter, sent to Lemon Squeezy, the payment
provider. Neither carries clipboard contents. ClipStack requests one macOS
permission, Accessibility, which is what allows it to paste into other apps.

## Who it is for

People who copy and paste constantly — developers, writers, designers,
support staff — and who lose time re-finding things they copied minutes ago.
